newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission proposes streamlined research programme.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission proposes streamlined research programme.

text.p: The European Commission proposed on Wednesday streamlining the EU's multibillion-dollar research programme to focus on projects that boost industrial competitiveness and improve the quality of life.
It said it was also proposing more flexible procedures for awarding money to the companies and research bodies that take on projects under the so-called Fifth Framework Programme.

The Commission said the programme, covering the period 1998-2002, should concentrate on six basic themes, including the ecosystem and telecommunications and computer technology that can create a "user-friendly information society".

It should also target "competitive and sustainable growth", supporting research, for example, into clean and "intelligent" products and manufacturing techniques, the Commission said in a statement. The bulk of the budget would cover research in those three areas, it said.
The rest would cover international research, training of scientists and innovation by small and medium-sized companies.
The proposal now goes to the Research Council and the European Parliament for approval.
EU Research Commissioner Edith Cresson told a news conference the Commission could not propose a budget, however, until governments had agreed a plan for future financing of EU activities.

But she said the total should represent at least the same percentage of the EU's gross national product as that of the existing research programme. The EU's 1994-98 research programme has a budget of 13.1 billion Ecus ($10 billion).
The more flexible procedures proposed by the Commission would, for example, set aside some untied money that could be mobilised when urgent research action was needed.
The Commission said that to speed up decision-making, it would like to take more of the day-to-day decisions that are now made by committees of national experts.

The Commission said it had taken on board some of the recommendations of a panel of experts, which said in February the EU's research programme needed a major overhaul. However, the panel's main complaint was that a requirement that all 15 countries adopt research programmes unanimously had hindered development of a pan-European strategy.

The EU would have to amend its treaty to change those procedures. The Commission has proposed that the inter-governmental conference change article 130i of the EC treaty, which now requires framework programmes to be adopted unanimously by thge Council in co-decision with the parliament.
